views.name: events_action_log_enriched
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  a.session AS session,
  a.user_id AS user_id,
  a.action AS action,
  a.category AS category,
  a.products AS products,
  a.amount AS amount,
  a.stamp AS stamp,
  u.sex AS sex,
  u.birth_date AS birth_date,
  u.register_date AS register_date,
  u.register_device AS register_device,
  u.withdraw_date AS withdraw_date
FROM action_log a
LEFT JOIN mst_users u
  ON a.user_id = u.user_id

params.description: Provides session-level action events enriched with user attributes so you can analyze user actions (what, when, amount, products) together with user demographics and registration/withdrawal info.
params.when_to_use: Count or list actions per session or per user with user attributes (sex, birth_date, register info). | Filter or group events by user attributes (sex, registration date) while preserving event-level detail (one row per session+stamp+action). | Join this event-level view into downstream aggregations (e.g., compute action counts or sum(amount) per user or per session) while treating the view as the event grain.
params.output_schema: session: session identifier for the event, derived from action_log.session | user_id: user identifier who performed the action, derived from action_log.user_id | action: action type/name recorded for the event, derived from action_log.action | category: action category recorded for the event, derived from action_log.category | products: product identifiers or payload associated with the action, derived from action_log.products | amount: numeric amount associated with the action (e.g., price/quantity), derived from action_log.amount | stamp: event timestamp for this action, derived from action_log.stamp | sex: user's sex/gender attribute, derived from mst_users.sex | birth_date: user's birth date, derived from mst_users.birth_date | register_date: user's registration date, derived from mst_users.register_date | register_device: device used at registration, derived from mst_users.register_device | withdraw_date: user's withdrawal/deactivation date, derived from mst_users.withdraw_date
params.grounded_columns: action_log.session | action_log.user_id | action_log.action | action_log.category | action_log.products | action_log.amount | action_log.stamp | mst_users.user_id | mst_users.sex | mst_users.birth_date | mst_users.register_date | mst_users.register_device | mst_users.withdraw_date
params.metric: amount = action_log.amount  -- event-level measure: use numeric amount directly from action_log | event_count = 1  -- implicit event grain: each row represents a single action event (one row per session+stamp+action)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to mst_users on action_log.user_id = mst_users.user_id — safe because this view already performs a LEFT JOIN to mst_users at a 1-to-1 (or many-to-1) cardinality from events to user; adding other user-level dimensions (mst_users or users_active_master) on user_id will not duplicate this view's event rows if the join key remains user_id and the joined table is 1 row per user. | do NOT join this view directly to one-to-many tables/views (for example, product-level line items if a single event.products expands to multiple product rows, or transaction-item tables) without re-aggregation, because such joins will multiply event rows and thus duplicate measures like amount and event_count. If you need per-product detail, first explode/aggregate products into a distinct product-level table (ensuring one row per event-product) or aggregate this view up to the desired grain (e.g., sum(amount) per session or per user) before joining. | If composing with sibling aggregation views (e.g., purchase_agg_per_user), prefer joining on user_id after aggregating this view to the same grain (e.g., group by user_id) so measures are aligned and not duplicated. | When joining to activity_sessions_latest or other session-level views, join on session (and optionally stamp) only if those views are guaranteed to be one-row-per-session (or one-row-per-session+stamp). If the other side is one-to-many per session, aggregate that side first or aggregate this view to session-level to avoid multiplication. | Safe composition patterns: (a) Aggregate this view to user-level (group by user_id) then join to user-level aggregates/ranks; (b) Aggregate to session-level (group by session) then join to session-level datasets; (c) Filter this view by user attributes (sex, register_date) — filtering does not change cardinality. | Unsafe composition patterns: direct join to products_latest_per_product, mst_products_latest_union, or any product-level ranking/line-item table on a product id extracted from products without first normalizing/expanding products — doing so may create many-to-many expansions and duplicate amounts/events unless you re-aggregate the results back to the event grain.

views.description: Event-level action_log joined to mst_users to expose user attributes alongside each action. Useful for analyses that need user demographics (sex, register_date, register_device) with each action event. | Use for: Segment actions by user demographic (e.g., actions by sex or register_device); Compute per-user or per-demographic aggregates of amount or event counts; Join to product or category masters after splitting products

views.name: users_active_master
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  user_id AS user_id,
  sex AS sex,
  birth_date AS birth_date,
  register_date AS register_date,
  register_device AS register_device,
  withdraw_date AS withdraw_date
FROM mst_users
WHERE withdraw_date IS NULL

params.description: A one-row-per-user view of currently active users (users with no withdraw_date) exposing core user attributes for downstream joins and filtering.
params.when_to_use: List or filter active users and their attributes (sex, birth_date, register_date, register_device). | As the user-side driving table when computing user-level metrics (e.g., lifetime purchases per active user) where you need exactly one row per active user. | To restrict analytic queries or joins to active users only before aggregating events or purchases. | To look up user attributes when enriching event or purchase aggregates that have been aggregated to user-level.
params.output_schema: user_id: unique user identifier (derived from mst_users.user_id). This is the grain of the view — one row per user_id. | sex: user's recorded sex/gender (derived from mst_users.sex). | birth_date: user's birth date (derived from mst_users.birth_date). | register_date: date the user registered (derived from mst_users.register_date). | register_device: device recorded at registration (derived from mst_users.register_device). | withdraw_date: NULL for active users (derived from mst_users.withdraw_date). The WHERE clause guarantees withdraw_date IS NULL for every row in this view.
params.grounded_columns: mst_users.user_id | mst_users.sex | mst_users.birth_date | mst_users.register_date | mst_users.register_device | mst_users.withdraw_date
params.metric: This view contains no aggregated metrics. All columns are direct base columns (no aggregates). | If you create derived user-level metrics on top of this view, define them as aggregates over events/purchases after joining to this one-row-per-user view (e.g., total_spend_per_user = SUM(purchase_amount) AFTER joining purchase_agg_per_user which is already aggregated per user).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to fact-aggregated or one-row-per-user views on user_id — e.g., join to purchase_agg_per_user on user_id — safe because purchase_agg_per_user is an aggregate per user (one row per user_id) so joining will not duplicate user-level measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to sibling rank/set views that are one-row-per-entity keyed by user_id (if such exist) on user_id — safe because they preserve one-row-per-user. | unsafe-to-join-without-reaggregation: do NOT join directly to raw/event-level one-to-many tables such as events_action_log_enriched on user_id unless you intend to multiply rows (the join will produce multiple event rows per user). If you need user-level metrics from events, first aggregate events to user level (e.g., events_action_log_enriched -> aggregate per user) and then join to this view. | unsafe-to-join-without-reaggregation: do NOT join directly to other one-to-many datasets (e.g., product sales or session-level tables like activity_sessions_latest if they are many-per-user) without first aggregating to the user grain, because that would duplicate this view's one row per user and lead to inflated measures. | planner guidance: because this view filters to mst_users.withdraw_date IS NULL, any joins that apply user-count denominators or user-level deduplication should be aware that the active-user predicate has already been applied; to compute metrics over all users (including withdrawn), use mst_users directly or another view that does not filter withdraw_date. | example safe composition pattern: users_active_master LEFT JOIN purchase_agg_per_user USING(user_id) — safe because users_active_master is one row per active user and purchase_agg_per_user is one row per user (no duplication). Aggregate after joining only when combining with many-sided datasets: e.g., users_active_master LEFT JOIN events_agg_per_user USING(user_id) then compute AVG(events_count) across users. | note on keys: the single primary key/grain is user_id. Any join preserving 1:1 or 1:0-1 cardinality on user_id will not duplicate rows; any join where the other side is 1:many must be reduced to 1:1 (aggregate/deduplicate) before joining if you wish to preserve correct user-level measures.

views.description: Subset of mst_users representing active users (not withdrawn). Use for cohorts restricted to currently active users. | Use for: Cohort analyses limited to active users; Retention and engagement metrics for users who haven't withdrawn

views.name: purchase_agg_per_user
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  user_id AS user_id,
  COUNT(purchase_id) AS purchase_count,
  SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
  CASE WHEN COUNT(purchase_id) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE AVG(amount) END AS average_amount,
  MAX(stamp) AS last_purchase_stamp
FROM purchase_log
GROUP BY user_id

params.description: Per-user purchase aggregates: count, sum, average and last purchase timestamp for each user.
params.when_to_use: Report total purchases, spend, average purchase amount, or last purchase date per user. | Filter or segment users by their purchase activity (e.g., users with >= N purchases or total spend > X). | Join to user-level dimensions to enrich user purchase metrics (e.g., user attributes or cohorts). | Serve as an aggregated base when composing higher-level queries (e.g., churn models, LTV cohorts) that need one row per user.
params.output_schema: user_id: user identifier; derived from purchase_log.user_id (GROUP BY user_id). | purchase_count: integer count of purchase events for the user; derived from COUNT(purchase_log.purchase_id). | total_amount: numeric total spend for the user; derived from SUM(purchase_log.amount). | average_amount: numeric average purchase amount for the user; derived from AVG(purchase_log.amount) but null when the user's purchase_count = 0 (SQL uses CASE WHEN COUNT(...) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE AVG(...) END). | last_purchase_stamp: latest purchase timestamp for the user; derived from MAX(purchase_log.stamp).
params.metric: purchase_count = COUNT(purchase_log.purchase_id)  -- per user count of purchase rows | total_amount = SUM(purchase_log.amount)  -- per user sum of amount | average_amount = CASE WHEN COUNT(purchase_log.purchase_id) = 0 THEN NULL ELSE AVG(purchase_log.amount) END  -- per user average amount with explicit null for zero purchases | last_purchase_stamp = MAX(purchase_log.stamp)  -- per user most recent purchase timestamp
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to users_active_master on user_id — safe because users_active_master is a user-level (one-row-per-user) dimension, so joining preserves one row per user and does NOT duplicate this view's measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to events_action_log_enriched on user_id only if events_action_log_enriched has been pre-aggregated to one row per user (otherwise it is one-to-many and will duplicate measures). If events_action_log_enriched is one-row-per-user, the join is safe. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views such as product_sales_ranked, products_latest_per_product, mst_products_latest_union, or activity_sessions_latest without re-aggregation because those are ranked/one-to-many per product or per session and will multiply this view's measures. If you must combine with such tables, first aggregate them to one row per user (or perform the join inside a query that re-aggregates results by user) to avoid duplicating purchase_count, total_amount, average_amount, and last_purchase_stamp. | If you need to join on other keys (e.g., product_id) ensure you aggregate the one-to-many side to user_id before joining so that this view's per-user measures remain cardinality-safe. | Planner hint: this AGG view is strictly one row per purchase_log.user_id. Any join to a dimension that is one-to-one or many-to-one into this user_id is safe; any join to a many-to-one in the other direction (i.e., many rows per user) must be aggregated first to avoid multiplying aggregated measures.

views.description: Aggregated purchase metrics per user: total purchases, total amount, average amount, last purchase timestamp. Useful for LTV, RFM, and user-level purchase summaries. | Use for: Compute user LTV or segmentation (RFM); Join purchase summaries to user demographics or event behavior

views.name: product_sales_ranked
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  product_id AS product_id,
  category_name AS category_name,
  sales AS sales,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category_name ORDER BY sales DESC) AS sales_rank
FROM product_sales

params.description: For each product within its category, returns the product's total sales and its rank by sales inside that category.
params.when_to_use: Find the top-N products by sales within each category (e.g., top 5 per category). | Label products with their position by sales inside their category for reporting or filtering (e.g., show only rank = 1). | Compose into dashboards or SQL that needs per-category product rank as an attribute (e.g., join to product details or user purchases). | Use as a pre-ranked input to further aggregation that groups by category_name and sales_rank (e.g., count how many products occupy each rank).
params.output_schema: product_id: the product identifier, derived directly from product_sales.product_id | category_name: the product's category name, derived directly from product_sales.category_name | sales: the sales measure for that product, derived directly from product_sales.sales | sales_rank: the rank (RANK window function) of the product within its category ordered by sales DESC, computed from product_sales.sales partitioned by product_sales.category_name
params.metric: sales = product_sales.sales | sales_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY product_sales.category_name ORDER BY product_sales.sales DESC)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-product dimension such as mst_products_latest_union or products_latest_per_product (on product_id) — safe because product_sales_ranked is one-row-per (category_name, product_id), so joining on product_id to a single-row-per-product view does NOT duplicate this view's measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to users_active_master on no direct key (not typical) is safe only if the join is one-to-one; avoid joining product_sales_ranked directly to users or events without constraining or aggregating the other side. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views such as events_action_log_enriched or purchase_agg_per_user (if those are one-to-many by product_id) without re-aggregating the many-side to one row per product_id (or per category_name, product_id). Joining a one-to-many child will multiply product_sales_ranked rows and will therefore duplicate the sales measure and invalidate ranks unless you re-aggregate after the join. | If you need to combine with activity_sessions_latest or other RANK/SET/AGG sibling views, ensure you join on keys that preserve uniqueness: e.g., to attach most-recent session info per product (if applicable), first reduce sessions to one-row-per-product_id. If joining on (category_name, product_id) is used and the other view is one-row-per-(category_name,product_id), the join is safe. | When composing further aggregations that sum sales, treat sales in this view as already at the (category_name, product_id) grain. If you join additional one-to-many facts, either (a) aggregate the many-side to that same grain before join, or (b) join and then re-aggregate grouping back to (category_name, product_id) to avoid double-counting. | When filtering by sales_rank (e.g., WHERE sales_rank <= 5) before joining out to other tables, that filter is stable — the rank is computed at the view grain and can be used to restrict rows safely prior to further joins or aggregations.

views.description: Product-level sales with a rank ordered by sales within each category. Exposes rank so downstream queries can filter top-N per category by WHERE rank <= N. | Use for: Top-N products by sales within each category; Compare rank changes when joining to another time snapshot

views.name: mst_products_latest_union
views.body_sql:
SELECT product_id AS product_id, name AS name, price AS price, updated_at AS updated_at, 'mst_products_20161201' AS source_table
FROM mst_products_20161201
UNION ALL
SELECT product_id AS product_id, name AS name, price AS price, updated_at AS updated_at, 'mst_products_20170101' AS source_table
FROM mst_products_20170101

params.description: Provides the latest unioned product records from two historical product tables, returning one row per product occurrence per source table.
params.when_to_use: Look up product attributes (name, price, updated_at) as stored in either historical source table for a given product_id and source_table identifier. | Compose analyses that need to compare or union product snapshots from the two source tables by product_id and source_table. | Build upstream aggregations or joins where product-level details from a specific source snapshot are required (for example, joining product attributes to sales rows that include a source_table tag).
params.output_schema: product_id: product identifier — derived from mst_products_20161201.product_id and mst_products_20170101.product_id | name: product name — derived from mst_products_20161201.name and mst_products_20170101.name | price: product price (as stored in the source snapshot) — derived from mst_products_20161201.price and mst_products_20170101.price | updated_at: timestamp when the product row was last updated in the source snapshot — derived from mst_products_20161201.updated_at and mst_products_20170101.updated_at | source_table: literal tag indicating which source table this row came from ('mst_products_20161201' or 'mst_products_20170101') — derived from the UNION ALL SELECT literals
params.grounded_columns: mst_products_20161201.product_id | mst_products_20161201.name | mst_products_20161201.price | mst_products_20161201.updated_at | mst_products_20170101.product_id | mst_products_20170101.name | mst_products_20170101.price | mst_products_20170101.updated_at
params.metric: product_id = identity column (no aggregation) — taken directly from source tables' product_id | name = identity column (no aggregation) — taken directly from source tables' name | price = identity column (no aggregation) — taken directly from source tables' price | updated_at = identity column (no aggregation) — taken directly from source tables' updated_at | source_table = constant literal per UNION branch ('mst_products_20161201' or 'mst_products_20170101')
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension/lookup tables that are 1:1 or many-to-1 on product_id (for example a products_latest_per_product view if it is one-row-per-product) using product_id — safe because mst_products_latest_union is at most one row per (product_id, source_table) and such joins will not duplicate these rows unless the dimension itself is multi-row per product_id. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to users_active_master or other user-level tables only when you have a clear linking key (e.g., user-specific key) — these are unrelated by product_id and should only be joined when a correct relationship exists. | unsafe join warning: do NOT freely join mst_products_latest_union to one-to-many tables (for example raw sales events, purchase_agg_per_user without appropriate grouping, or events_action_log_enriched) on product_id without first aggregating the many-side to one row per (product_id, source_table) or otherwise controlling multiplicity, because those joins will multiply rows from this view and thereby duplicate its per-row attributes. | unsafe join warning: do NOT join to sibling ranked or session views (product_sales_ranked, activity_sessions_latest) unless those sibling views are known to be one-row-per-product_id (or per the same (product_id, source_table) grain) — ranked and latest views often contain ties or multiple rows and can duplicate measures. | composition tip: to safely compute product-level aggregates that combine this view with many-sided event/sales data, first aggregate the many-sided table to one row per (product_id, source_table) or per product_id (matching the chosen grain), then join. Example safe pattern: WITH sales_per_product AS (SELECT product_id, source_table, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales_events GROUP BY product_id, source_table) SELECT p.product_id, p.name, s.total_sales FROM mst_products_latest_union p LEFT JOIN sales_per_product s USING (product_id, source_table); | grain note: this view's explicit grain is (product_id, source_table). Do not assume it is de-duplicated to one row per product_id alone — multiple source_table values may exist for the same product_id.

views.description: Union of product master snapshots (mst_products_20161201, mst_products_20170101) with source_stamp to track origin. Useful for analyzing product changes across snapshots and selecting the latest record per product. | Use for: Identify product attribute changes over time; Select the latest product record per product_id using a RANK over updated_at

views.name: products_latest_per_product
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  product_id AS product_id,
  name AS name,
  price AS price,
  updated_at AS updated_at
FROM (
  SELECT
    product_id,
    name,
    price,
    updated_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM (
    SELECT product_id, name, price, updated_at FROM mst_products_20161201
    UNION ALL
    SELECT product_id, name, price, updated_at FROM mst_products_20170101
  )
) WHERE rn = 1

params.description: Latest snapshot per product: returns the most recent row (by updated_at) for each product_id across two source snapshots.
params.when_to_use: Lookup the current/latest attributes (name, price, updated_at) for a given product_id or set of product_ids. | Join product dimensional attributes onto fact/aggregate datasets when each product should contribute at most one row. | Compose higher-level aggregations that need the latest product price (e.g., latest price-weighted metrics) by treating this view as the canonical one-row-per-product price source.
params.output_schema: product_id: unique product identifier (derived from mst_products_20161201.product_id and mst_products_20170101.product_id, chosen as the partition key for ROW_NUMBER to pick latest row) | name: product name string for the latest snapshot (derived from mst_products_20161201.name or mst_products_20170101.name — the value from the row with the highest updated_at is returned) | price: product price for the latest snapshot (derived from mst_products_20161201.price or mst_products_20170101.price — the value from the row with the highest updated_at is returned) | updated_at: timestamp of the source row selected as latest (derived from mst_products_20161201.updated_at or mst_products_20170101.updated_at; used to determine recency)
params.grounded_columns: mst_products_20161201.product_id | mst_products_20161201.name | mst_products_20161201.price | mst_products_20161201.updated_at | mst_products_20170101.product_id | mst_products_20170101.name | mst_products_20170101.price | mst_products_20170101.updated_at
params.metric: product_id = product_id (identity, the grain column) | name = latest_row.name (non-aggregated attribute chosen by ORDER BY updated_at DESC with ROW_NUMBER partitioned by product_id) | price = latest_row.price (non-aggregated attribute chosen by ORDER BY updated_at DESC with ROW_NUMBER partitioned by product_id) | updated_at = latest_row.updated_at (timestamp used to determine latest row)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension or lookup tables that are one-row-per-product (e.g., a products master table with unique product_id) on product_id — safe because this view is one-row-per-product_id and such joins will not multiply rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to event/fact tables (one-to-many) on product_id only when the downstream query handles the one-to-many relationship correctly (for example, by aggregating the fact table first or by using DISTINCT/row_number logic). Directly joining this view to a one-to-many fact without re-aggregation will produce one output row per fact row and will not duplicate this view's rows but will expand them to match facts — this is expected but not safe if you intend to preserve one-row-per-product. | do NOT join to one-to-many tables/views (e.g., events_action_log_enriched, activity_sessions_latest if those are multi-row per product) when you rely on this view's per-product measure semantics unless you re-aggregate after the join. Joining directly to a many-side will cause product rows to repeat for each matching many-side row and will multiply any measures that assume single row per product. | safe composition with aggregations: if you need product-level aggregates after joining to a many-side, apply GROUP BY product_id (or aggregate the many-side first into one row per product) to restore one-row-per-product semantics before joining other one-row-per-product dimensions. | planner note about the RANK pattern: this view materializes a deterministic one-row-per-product by using ROW_NUMBER() partitioned on product_id ordered by updated_at DESC and filtering rn = 1, so any join on product_id to this view is stable (one output row per product_id) provided the other side is at most one row per product_id or is pre-aggregated.

views.description: Latest product record per product_id from the unioned product snapshots. Use when you need a single canonical product row (latest updated_at) for joins with events. | Use for: Join events to a single current product master; Report current price or name for product-level revenue calculations

views.name: activity_sessions_latest
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  session AS session,
  stamp AS stamp,
  action AS action,
  option AS option,
  path AS path,
  search_type AS search_type
FROM (
  SELECT
    session,
    stamp,
    action,
    option,
    path,
    search_type,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY session ORDER BY stamp DESC) AS rn
  FROM activity_log
)
WHERE rn = 1

params.description: Latest activity log row per session (most-recent stamp and its associated action/option/path/search_type).
params.when_to_use: Get the most recent activity details for each session (session-level latest action and metadata). | Join latest session activity to user/session-level tables to analyze user behavior at session end or latest event. | Compose into aggregates that need the most recent action per session (e.g., count of sessions by last action). | Filter sessions by their latest action or path before joining to other datasets.
params.output_schema: session: session identifier for the session (derived from activity_log.session) | stamp: timestamp of the activity row selected as the latest for that session (derived from activity_log.stamp) | action: action name/type from the latest activity row for that session (derived from activity_log.action) | option: option metadata from the latest activity row for that session (derived from activity_log.option) | path: page/path or URL recorded for the latest activity row for that session (derived from activity_log.path) | search_type: search_type value from the latest activity row for that session (derived from activity_log.search_type)
params.grounded_columns: activity_log.session | activity_log.stamp | activity_log.action | activity_log.option | activity_log.path | activity_log.search_type
params.metric: This view is strictly a row-level projection of the latest row per session. No aggregated metrics are produced here. | If you need counts or other aggregates derived from this view, compute them explicitly, e.g. latest_session_count = COUNT(session) aggregated over this view.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to users_active_master on session -> user/session key (safe) — this view is one-row-per-session, so joining to a one-row-per-session-or-user master table will not duplicate latest-session rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to purchase_agg_per_user on session.user_id = purchase_agg_per_user.user_id — safe if purchase_agg_per_user is aggregated one-row-per-user (no duplication of session rows when joining by user), but be mindful that multiple sessions map to the same user (that multiplies user-level metrics across sessions intentionally). | DO NOT join directly to one-to-many event/detail tables such as events_action_log_enriched without aggregating the child table first — joining to a one-to-many table will duplicate this view's one-row-per-session rows and thus multiply any derived counts or metrics. | DO NOT join to product_sales_ranked or products_latest_per_product (ranked or per-product views that are one-row-per-product) unless you join by a product key present in this view (this view does not contain a product key), otherwise the join will produce a Cartesian-like expansion. | If you need to combine with many-rows-per-session sources, first aggregate those sources to one-row-per-session (e.g., counts, sums, latest timestamps) and then join to this view to preserve cardinality. | When composing aggregates: treat this view as the session grain. Any measure that should remain at the session grain must be computed from this view or from sources aggregated to session grain before joining. | Example safe pattern: SELECT a.session, a.action, p.total_purchases FROM activity_sessions_latest a JOIN (SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_purchases FROM purchase_agg_per_user GROUP BY user_id) p ON a.user_id = p.user_id — only safe if activity_sessions_latest is extended to include user_id or you join via a correct key that is one-to-one or many-to-one in the intended direction.

views.description: Latest activity event per session (most recent stamp). Useful to identify session end time or last action for session-level summarization. | Use for: Sessionization and session-level metrics; Join latest session activity to user_id via action_log or access_log
